standard.title: Science responses impact society
standard.description: examine how proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues may impact on society and explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can investigate how individuals and communities use scientific knowledge to identify problems and make decisions (AC9S5H02). They have not yet examined how proposed scientific responses to issues carry ethical, environmental, social and economic trade-offs.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine how proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues may impact on society and explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations.

nodes.label: Scientific responses to contemporary issues
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify proposed scientific responses to contemporary issues and describe the intended impact
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of a proposed scientific response to a contemporary issue; describe the problem it addresses and the intended impact
nodes.typical_width: Compare two proposed scientific responses to the same or related issues; explain how each addresses the problem differently
wider: Investigate how laboratory-grown meat is proposed as a response to ecosystem impacts of livestock farming
Examine how desalination plants are proposed as a response to freshwater scarcity
Research how ecological reserves are proposed as a response to biodiversity loss and competing land use interests

response_modes.reason: Students need a repertoire of scientific response examples across different issue types — food production, water scarcity, biodiversity — to be able to reason about impacts across contexts in later nodes. A single example limits the range of consideration types students can encounter; multiple examples build the conceptual library needed for the four-lens analysis in Node 3.

success_criteria: Identifies a proposed scientific response and the contemporary issue it addresses
Describes the intended impact of the response
Distinguishes the scientific response from a political or social response

nodes.label: Impacts can be positive and negative
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine both intended and unintended impacts of a scientific response on society and the environment
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one intended and one unintended impact of a proposed scientific response; explain why the unintended impact occurs
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the impacts of a scientific response across environmental and social dimensions; explain how an intended benefit in one area can create an unintended cost in another
wider: Examine how desalination plants produce fresh water but impact marine ecosystems at discharge sites
Investigate how changes in aircraft design improved safety and efficiency but introduced environmental considerations
Research how the introduction of biological controls solved one problem but created new ecological impacts

response_modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate scientific responses as simply 'good' or 'bad' rather than examining trade-offs. Seeing multiple examples where the same response produces both positive and negative impacts — desalination, aircraft design, biological controls — across different contexts helps students develop nuanced evaluation rather than binary judgement. Single-context teaching entrenches the binary view.

success_criteria: Identifies both an intended and an unintended impact of a scientific response
Explains why the unintended impact occurs
Does not frame the response as simply good or bad

nodes.label: Ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations associated with a proposed scientific response
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two types of consideration (from ethical, environmental, social, economic) relevant to a proposed scientific response; explain why each matters
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a proposed scientific response across all four consideration types; explain why stakeholders may hold different views depending on which consideration they prioritise
wider: Investigate the ethical, environmental, social and economic implications of others using First Nations Australians' knowledges of medicinal properties of endemic plants
Investigate ethical and economic implications of cross-cultural partnerships that build on First Nations Australians' land management techniques
Research how properties of gases were used in WWI gas warfare and the subsequent development of international arms control treaties — examine the ethical implications

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate the four consideration types or address only one (usually environmental). Examining the same response through all four lenses across different contexts — medicinal plants, land management, gas warfare — helps students distinguish the considerations and understand why different stakeholders prioritise differently. Breadth across contexts is what builds the four-lens thinking habit.

The four-lens analysis requires an explicit reasoning scaffold — students need to be supported in applying each consideration type systematically rather than defaulting to whichever lens feels most prominent. Without structure, students describe one consideration in depth and mention others superficially.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The medicinal plants and land management directions are rich — they introduce biopiracy, intellectual property, and cross-cultural partnership as ethical dimensions that go well beyond standard environmental ethics. Advancing students who investigate these cases encounter genuinely complex ethical territory that connects to real contemporary debates about Indigenous knowledge rights.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two types of consideration relevant to a specific response
Explains why each consideration matters for that response
Distinguishes between the consideration types rather than conflating them

nodes.label: Evaluating scientific responses with multiple considerations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine a proposed scientific response by weighing multiple considerations and explaining why stakeholders may reach different conclusions
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one proposed scientific response using at least two consideration types; explain why different stakeholders may evaluate it differently
nodes.typical_width: Compare how two different stakeholder groups evaluate the same scientific response; explain how their different priorities lead to different conclusions
wider: Evaluate a proposed ecological reserve by analysing competing interests — conservation scientists, landowners, First Nations communities, local government — and explain what each prioritises
Analyse the development of laboratory-grown meat from the perspective of farmers, environmentalists, consumers and ethicists
Construct an evidence-based argument for or against a proposed scientific response, explicitly addressing counter-arguments from stakeholders with different priorities

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the response identification (Node 1), trade-off analysis (Node 2), and four-lens framework (Node 3) into a coordinated stakeholder evaluation. Students who can apply each element separately but cannot coordinate them into a multi-stakeholder analysis have not met the descriptor's full evaluative demand.

The argument-construction direction — arguing for or against a response while addressing counter-arguments — requires explicit scaffolding of the claim-evidence-counterargument structure. Students need support both in selecting and weighting considerations and in representing opposing stakeholder positions fairly rather than as straw men.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The ecological reserve direction — four distinct stakeholder groups with genuinely competing interests including First Nations communities — is rich for advancing students. It models real-world scientific decision-making complexity and gives students practice with genuine stakeholder plurality rather than two-sided debate format.
success_criteria: Examines a scientific response using at least two consideration types
Explains why different stakeholders evaluate the response differently
Connects stakeholder conclusions to their priorities rather than framing disagreement as ignorance
